passages.t: ‘Have mercy on me, O God’: the heading, and ‘Against You, You only, have I sinned’
passages.happening:
The heading sets the scene. “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. When Nathan the prophet came to him after his adultery with Bathsheba” (verse 1).

David does not begin with excuses. He begins with God's character. “Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your loving devotion; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions” (verse 1). He uses three words for what he has done: transgressions, iniquity and sin (verses 1 and 2). He asks God to blot them out, wash him and cleanse him.

He hides nothing. “For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me” (verse 3). “Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight, so that You may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge” (verse 4).

Then he looks back to the start of his life. “Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me” (verse 5). And he looks within: “Surely You desire truth in the inmost being” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The heading points to 2 Samuel 11 and 12, and it is right to say plainly what happened. King David saw Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, one of his soldiers, while Uriah was away at war. “Then David sent messengers to get her” (2 Samuel 11:4). He was the king, and he used his power over her. She became pregnant. To hide what he had done, David sent a letter to his commander: “Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed” (2 Samuel 11:15). Uriah died.

The Bible puts the blame on David. “But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD” (2 Samuel 11:27). Nathan told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb, and then said, “You are that man!” (2 Samuel 12:7). Nothing in the story or the psalm blames Bathsheba.

The three words of verses 1 and 2 cover the whole range of wrong: crossing a line on purpose, a twisted act, and missing the mark. ‘Blot out’ is the language of wiping a record clean.

The book page explains what the headings are, and that readers weigh them differently. Psalm 51 is one of the seven psalms the church has long called the penitential psalms, prayers of sorrow for sin.
passages.later:
When Nathan confronted him, David said, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan answered, “The LORD has taken away your sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).

Paul quotes verse 4 in Romans 3:4, in a slightly different form from the Greek: “So that You may be proved right when You speak and victorious when You judge” (Romans 3:4). His point is the psalm's point. When people are found false, God is still right.

Jesus told of a tax collector who could only pray, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). That man, Jesus said, went home right with God.
passages.hard:
Two lines here are hard.

‘Against You, You only, have I sinned’ (verse 4). How can David say that, when he wronged Bathsheba and had Uriah killed? He is not saying that they were not harmed. In 2 Samuel 12 he accepts Nathan's charge about Uriah without arguing. Most readers take the verse to mean that every wrong done to a person is, at its root, also a wrong against God, who made that person and whose law protects them. Joseph said the same when he refused his master's wife: “how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” (Genesis 39:9). Others hear a courtroom: God is the only judge who can give the verdict, so the confession is made to him. None of these readings makes the harm to Uriah and Bathsheba smaller. They put it in front of God.

‘I was brought forth in iniquity’ (verse 5). The book page lists this among the hard passages. Christians have read it in different ways. Many in the Western church, following Augustine, read it as teaching original sin: that since Adam every person is born with a nature already bent toward sin, and some add that they share Adam's guilt (Romans 5:12). Orthodox Christians speak of ancestral sin: we inherit death and a pull toward sin, but not guilt. Others read the verse as a poem's way of saying that David's sin goes all the way down, as far back as he has been alive. Whichever reading is right, the ‘I’ of the verse is David. It does not say that his mother sinned by conceiving him, that the love of husband and wife is sinful, or that a baby is anything less than precious to God.
passages.asks:
David's prayer has no ‘but’. He does not say ‘but she’, or ‘but the pressure’, or ‘but everyone does it’. He names it, and he leans his whole weight on God's mercy.

If guilt is heavy on you, this is the place to begin. The promise is real: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

If you have been harmed by someone with power over you, hear this too. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Bible did not blame Bathsheba, and it does not blame you. Please tell someone you trust. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

passages.t: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God’, and ‘take not Your Holy Spirit from me’
passages.happening:
Now David asks to be made clean. “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow” (verse 7). He asks, “let the bones You have crushed rejoice” (verse 8). “Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities” (verse 9).

Then the centre of the psalm. “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (verse 10).

He is afraid of one thing above all. “Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me” (verse 11). And he asks for joy again. “Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Hyssop was a small plant with bushy stems, used to sprinkle in rites of cleansing. At the first Passover it was used to put the lamb's blood on the doorframes (Exodus 12:22). It was also used to cleanse someone healed of a skin disease, or someone who had touched the dead. A priest did the sprinkling. David asks God to do it himself.

‘Create’ is the Hebrew bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, where God creates the heavens and the earth. In the Bible only God is ever the subject of this verb. David does not ask for a better effort. He asks for a new heart that only God can make.

Why fear losing God's Spirit? David had seen it happen. When Samuel anointed David, “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David” (1 Samuel 16:13). The very next verse says, “After the Spirit of the LORD had departed from Saul, a spirit of distress from the LORD began to torment him” (1 Samuel 16:14). David had watched the king before him lose God's Spirit. He was afraid of becoming Saul.

The words ‘Holy Spirit’ appear only here and in Isaiah 63:10-11 in the whole Old Testament.
passages.later:
God promised through Ezekiel, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). David's prayer is a request for what God later promised to his whole people.

Isaiah heard the same offer: “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18). The letter to the Hebrews says that what hyssop and animal blood pointed to, Christ does: “how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered Himself unblemished to God, purify our consciences from works of death” (Hebrews 9:14).
passages.hard: Can a Christian today lose the Holy Spirit? Christians answer this in different ways. Many point out that in the Old Testament the Spirit often came on people for a task, such as being king, and could be withdrawn, as with Saul. After Pentecost, they say, Jesus' promise is that the Spirit will be with his people forever (John 14:16), and Paul says believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13). Other Christians, in traditions that teach that a believer can fall away, take the verse as a serious warning still. Christians have long discussed this, and it is not a cause for division. Many believers of every view still pray verse 11, as a cry not to drift from God.
passages.asks:
Verse 10 asks for more than forgiveness. It asks to be changed. Being forgiven is the start. Being made new is the work God goes on doing.

Notice what David wants back in verse 12. Not his reputation, not his comfort. ‘The joy of Your salvation.’ Sin had taken the joy. He asks God to give it back.

passages.t: ‘A broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise’
passages.happening:
Forgiven people have something to say. “Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You” (verse 13).

David names his worst guilt directly. “Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation” (verse 14). He asks God even for the words to praise him. “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise” (verse 15).

Then he says what God really wants. “For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise” (verses 16 and 17).

The psalm ends with a prayer for the city: “build up the walls of Jerusalem” (verse 18). Then sacrifices will please God again (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
‘Bloodguilt’ was the guilt of shedding innocent blood. Uriah's death stands behind the word.

The law of Moses gave sacrifices for many sins. But for sin done deliberately, in open defiance, no offering was listed. “But the person who sins defiantly, whether a native or foreigner, blasphemes the LORD. That person shall be cut off from among his people” (Numbers 15:30). That is why David says he has nothing to bring. Only mercy is left.

‘Contrite’ means crushed, broken in pieces. It is the opposite of a proud heart.

Verses 18 and 19 pray for Jerusalem's walls to be rebuilt. Many scholars think these lines were added later, in or after the exile, when the walls lay in ruins, so the whole people could pray David's prayer. Others read them as David's own prayer that his sin would not bring harm on his city. Both readings are held.
passages.later:
Peter, who also failed badly, was restored by Jesus and sent to care for others (John 21:15-17). David's ‘then I will teach transgressors’ became his life.

Jesus said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).
passages.asks:
God does not want a show of being sorry. He wants a broken heart: the real thing, without performance. And he promises not to despise it.

If you are afraid that what you have done is too much, notice who prayed this psalm. A king who abused his power and had a man killed. Psalm 51 has been prayed for many centuries by people who were sure they had gone too far. It is there for you too.
